report:
# Research Summary: Does Opening a Bedroom Window/Door Improve Sleep Quality?

**Verdict: Largely supported by evidence, with important caveats.**

Multiple controlled field studies converge on the same finding. A well-cited study by Mishra et al., published in *Indoor Air* and reanalyzed by DTU/Eindhoven researchers, monitored 17 young adults over five nights each with windows/doors open vs. closed. Open conditions produced significantly lower CO2 (avoiding buildup above ~1,000–1,150 ppm), and objectively measured actigraphy data plus subjective sleep diaries showed improved sleep latency, fewer awakenings, and better perceived sleep quality (onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/ina.12435).

A larger 2022 field intervention across 40 Danish bedrooms during heating season similarly found that opening windows reduced CO2, VOCs, and PM10, and both objectively and subjectively measured sleep quality improved, along with better next-day cognitive performance (sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132322008605).

Follow-up analyses (DTU, 2024) reinforce a dose-response relationship: keeping bedroom CO2 below roughly 1,000 ppm—achievable via ventilation—is associated with optimal sleep, and levels above that threshold degrade sleep quality (sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132323011459).

**Important caveats:** These benefits depend on outdoor conditions. Sources note that in areas with poor outdoor air quality, high pollen/allergen levels, or high ambient noise, opening a window can worsen sleep and health rather than help it (molekule.com/blogs/all/sleep-window-open-night). Climate (extreme cold/heat) and security/pest concerns are also relevant practical limitations.

**Bottom line:** The core mechanism—reduced CO2/improved air exchange via open windows or doors—has real experimental support from actigraphy-based studies, not just anecdote. However, it's a conditional truth: beneficial primarily when outdoor air is clean and quiet, not a universal rule.
